title: Alex Su and Andy Chagui on Flexible Legal Talent, AI Pressure, and the Future of Law Firm Leverage
author: Alex Su · Andy Chagui

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source offers relevant examples of human staffing, client vetting and caution about anecdotal AI market claims, but it does not directly assess whether multidisciplinary legal engineering, substantive verification and task-specific evaluation are necessary to convert AI capability into reliable legal services.
qs: So any candidate that we ever propose, we propose them to our law firm, and the law firm partner will have his or her opportunity to do their own vetting and make sure that they’re comfortable with this person’s qualifications, right, before they put them on sensitive matters for their clients.
But really what I always worry about is that when I read things in Bloomberg or ALM, I don’t know if it’s tied to reality.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts that pricing pressure and buyer incentives will reshape legal delivery, and materially extends the cluster by proposing “outsourced leverage”: partners retain judgment and accountability while AI and flexible talent replace some traditional associate support. It also reinforces the unresolved staffing and succession issue, expressly leaving associate numbers and future firm structure uncertain.
qs: My view is that with AI and technology and flexible talent, there’s a whole host of different tools you can use to support that partner.
Maybe it’s fewer, or maybe it stays the same and they’re just set up differently.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that AI and changing client demand may alter associate leverage and succession, while rejecting a simple disappearance narrative. It materially extends the cluster by proposing experienced flexible talent as outsourced leverage under continuing partner accountability and by illustrating AI-related knowledge-management work as a broader career route, though its support is anecdotal rather than systematic.
qs: Maybe it’s fewer, or maybe it stays the same and they’re just set up differently.

We just had one of our attorneys who was on assignment with one of our AmLaw 100 law firms helping the knowledge management team with some of these AI initiatives, and the law firm ended up making a permanent offer to our attorney to come and join the firm.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Su accepts the cluster’s core premise that AI’s value depends on redesigning legal production rather than merely acquiring technology. He adds a concrete model: combine AI, technology and flexible talent as “outsourced leverage” supporting senior partners, reprice junior work, and retain partner responsibility for vetting and client accountability. His contribution is grounded in reported client feedback and outsourcing precedent, not quantified evidence of broader effects.
qs: My view is that with AI and technology and flexible talent, there’s a whole host of different tools you can use to support that partner.
That doesn’t change the trust and accountability that that partner has to the client.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI will reconfigure legal production and associate leverage without eliminating lawyers, while senior judgment, trust and accountability remain valuable. It materially extends the cluster by proposing experienced flexible lawyers as “outsourced leverage”: a concrete hybrid staffing layer combining AI, technology and contingent talent to deliver the middle segment of work differently amid uncertain demand.
qs: My view is that with AI and technology and flexible talent, there’s a whole host of different tools you can use to support that partner.
That doesn’t change the trust and accountability that that partner has to the client.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will redesign staffing and task allocation rather than eliminate lawyers wholesale. It materially extends that proposition by presenting experienced flexible talent as “outsourced leverage” for variable demand and under-resourced AI projects, while retaining partner accountability. Its claims are grounded mainly in operating experience and anecdotes, not systematic evidence.
qs: My view is that with AI and technology and flexible talent, there’s a whole host of different tools you can use to support that partner.
Alex Su (26:31)  My instinct is that the associates won’t go away.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s principal shift from AI publicity toward practical, everyday use by lawyers. It supports the framing but provides no substantive evidence on workflow fit, adoption, renewal economics, consumption costs or control of the working environment.
qs: So Marlene, you know, the past couple of years, we’ve talked about a lot, or we’ve seen a lot about law firms that are putting out these press releases, talking about all the great stuff they’re doing with AI.
But really, we’re, you know, I think we’re at a phase right now where we’ve got to start looking at how attorneys are using this in their day-to-day practice.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s concern that existing billable-hour incentives obstruct developmental AI work and recognises the succession risk if associates are not trained into senior roles. It remains cautious about AI-driven headcount reductions and focuses more on flexible staffing than on reconstructing apprenticeship, so it does not materially extend the cluster’s proposed training response.
qs: But when the practical reality is that an associate who’s behind in their hours gets faced with needing to either find billable work or work on something that’s extra credit that they do get some credit for, I think what you end up finding is that a lot of the associates choose the billable work.

Because if you’re not getting the succession of associates that kind of move into partner level, and they’re not being sort of trained in that capacity, what happens when you have that generation pass the baton?

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports selective, context-driven learning: Su and Chagui combine published material with recurring client and partner conversations to test market narratives rather than simply follow AI news or product releases. Their evidence is explicitly anecdotal, matching the cluster’s caution that professional networks provide useful contextual intelligence but do not systematically validate trends.
qs: But really what I always worry about is that when I read things in Bloomberg or ALM, I don’t know if it’s tied to reality.
And so Andy and the other partners at Latitude will kind of give me anecdotes, will tell us like, hey, this is the conversation we’ve had with the GC or a law firm partner this week.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI does not automatically displace human judgment or settle legal pricing outcomes. It defends senior partners’ continuing advisory value while treating any decline in their hourly rates as uncertain; its client-conversation evidence remains professional observation rather than measured market evidence.
qs: They are providing legitimate valuable guidance and so that’s not going to change.
So even though there’s a lot of AI change, I don’t know that the hourly rate of the top partners will go down.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal distinction between proliferating AI announcements and meaningful evidence of day-to-day use. It reinforces the need to examine practical adoption rather than publicity, but provides no concrete findings on implementation, outcomes or vendor selection.

kp.k: Flexible talent supplements rather than necessarily replaces traditional staffing
kp.d: Su and Chagui describe experienced contract lawyers as another resource for law firms and corporate legal departments, rather than endorsing the host’s suggestion that growing demand proves the pyramid is broken. Chagui reports assignments covering secondments, leave, hiring gaps and projects, with law firm clients ranging from boutiques to AmLaw 50 firms. These are provider accounts of their business, not independently measured market findings.
qs: Yeah, I would say it’s just another resource for firms.
We’re a big believer in pairing the right resource with the right type of work, no matter who our client is.
And we help law firms of every size, from boutique firms all the way up to AmLaw 50 law firms.

kp.k: Remote work expands access to experienced, senior-level contract lawyers
kp.d: Su reports placements doing associate-, counsel- and partner-level work, including first-chairing a trial. Chagui tentatively links expanded availability to post-COVID acceptance of remote work and says most Latitude lawyers have 10-plus years of experience, enabling deployment for three-, six- or nine-month needs without the mentoring required by less experienced associates.
qs: We’ve gotten placements where we have someone first-chairing a trial, as an example.
I mean, after COVID, certainly when remote work became so popular, I think that really kind of changed things.
Most of our attorneys come with 10-plus years of experience.

kp.k: AI implementation creates demand for experienced legal subject-matter experts
kp.d: Chagui reports that Big Law knowledge management and innovation teams need additional people to implement AI and support practice-specific uses, despite having purchased tools. Relatively small teams face fluctuating workloads that may not justify permanent hires. He describes contract lawyers training internal platforms, conducting market studies and verifying AI output for accuracy; these are reported engagements, not quantified evidence of AI performance or return on investment.
qs: We need the subject matter experts to help us with all of these initiatives.
And so they don’t have the resources because even though they’re large law firms, the knowledge management or innovation teams are relatively small.

Our attorneys are serving as subject matter experts themselves, training the platforms and then reviewing the output and doing quality control to make sure that the information that the AI is generating is actually accurate.

kp.k: Billable incentives impede internal AI development and training
kp.d: Chagui says firms struggled to staff AI projects with associates because nonbillable work lost priority to client work and carried high opportunity costs. Asked about firms offering 50 to 200 hours of credit for AI learning, Su calls credit a positive step but argues associates behind on hours still tend to choose billable work. His conclusion draws on observed demand for supplemental staffing rather than a comparison of credit policies.
qs: The problem with that, as you can imagine, is that it’s not billable work, right? So the associates are prioritizing the billable work.
The opportunity cost there is very high, and the associates aren’t giving the attention that it deserves.
I think it’s a step in the right direction, but it can be really hard because it’s just a tough spot for the associate.

kp.k: Project work enables AI specialisms and alternative legal careers
kp.d: Su argues that remote engagement-based work lets lawyers combine narrow assignments across clients into specialisms that previously could not sustain a single full-time position, including expertise in newer AI tools. Chagui reports one lawyer’s move from a Latitude assignment supporting an AmLaw 100 knowledge management team’s AI initiatives to a permanent firm role. The lawyer’s reported satisfaction is an individual customer-provider anecdote, not general career-outcome evidence.
qs: So somebody can develop an expertise in a specific area and maybe do certain types of work that wouldn’t be able to be supported by a full-time role in the past, but now they can specialize in it.
An example of that is working with some of these newer AI tools, specializing in technology that hasn’t been around for very long.

We just had one of our attorneys who was on assignment with one of our AmLaw 100 law firms helping the knowledge management team with some of these AI initiatives, and the law firm ended up making a permanent offer to our attorney to come and join the firm.

kp.k: Hiring uncertainty strengthens the case for flexible staffing
kp.d: Su explicitly declines to predict AI’s effect on associate numbers. He argues that forecasting practice-area demand three or four years before entry has long produced overhiring, layoffs and subsequent midlevel shortages. He expects uncertainty to increase demand for alternative resources, including practitioners with 10 or 20 years of experience who can fill gaps quickly with limited oversight.
qs: And the firms are making decisions on hiring and demand for different practice areas three or four years in advance.
So I don’t know what’s going to happen with AI and associates, but what I can tell you is that it’s not a new thing for firms to misinterpret future demand signals.
So as we see more uncertainty unfold, I would expect greater demand for different resources.

kp.k: Contingent staffing absorbs volatile demand without permanent hiring commitments
kp.d: Chagui describes scaling contract staffing up and down rather than overcommitting to full-time associates. As an example, he reports one firm using dozens of Latitude lawyers to support a rainmaker’s high-volume work that might last six months or end unexpectedly. The host additionally frames flexible staffing as a response to the reputational stigma of law firm layoffs; that framing is not separately substantiated.
qs: I mean, we allow the firms to be able to have the flexibility to scale up and scale down as needed, right? As opposed to overcommitting on full-time hires.

You know, we have one law firm that has dozens of our Latitude attorneys working for the firm, helping a very busy big-time rainmaker at the firm with high-volume work that may last for the next six months or may go away unexpectedly, right?

kp.k: AI and outsourced leverage challenge junior-work pricing
kp.d: Su reports that clients object less to expensive partners than to first- and second-year lawyer charges. He argues that senior judgment on high-value matters may be underpriced, while work beneath partners is mispriced. He proposes AI, technology and flexible lawyers as alternative resources supporting partners, describing contract lawyers as outsourced leverage rather than full-time associates. This is a commercial argument informed by reported client conversations, not measured pricing evidence.
qs: What I hear from clients is that they don’t have any issues paying the partner who’s expensive. They have issues paying the first or second year.
My view is that with AI and technology and flexible talent, there’s a whole host of different tools you can use to support that partner.
And so one of my colleagues has called it outsourced leverage. That’s what we provide.

kp.k: Outsourcing leaves partner accountability and candidate vetting intact
kp.d: Su argues that client trust remains attached to the partner even when work is delegated externally, using outsourced first-level document review as an existing analogy. Chagui says both Latitude and the hiring firm vet candidates before sensitive assignments. These are descriptions of responsibility and selection practices, not claims that outsourcing eliminates quality risks.
qs: But in terms of who that work gets passed to, that is on the firm and the partner to vet.
That doesn’t change the trust and accountability that that partner has to the client.
It was just Alex’s prior point about the vetting, that not only does Latitude do the vetting, but our law firm clients also do their own vetting, right?

kp.k: Associate succession remains unresolved rather than destined for elimination
kp.d: Responding to concerns about training future partners, Su says associates probably will remain, but their numbers, configuration or attrition could change. He recalls a summer class of a hundred in which he thinks only one became partner, illustrating existing attrition rather than an AI effect. He urges firm leadership to consider succession amid flexible staffing, generative AI and agentic AI, without specifying a future staffing shape.
qs: My instinct is that the associates won’t go away. Maybe it’s fewer, or maybe it stays the same and they’re just set up differently.
Like, I remember when I was a summer associate, we started with a hundred people in my summer class. I think that only one of us made partner.
And I don’t think it’s just Flex Talent or us. It’s certainly AI, not just generative AI, but now agentic AI.

kp.k: In-house budget pressure drives demands for provider AI strategies
kp.d: Su reports that some companies require firms and providers to develop AI strategies as a condition of future work, while others wait to see what proves effective. He predicts medium- to long-term business-model change as legal departments seek more work within limited budgets and allocate matters among providers. Although the host asks about actual insourcing, Su supplies no specific completed AI-driven insourcing example.
qs: Some companies that we talk to are explicitly telling the firms and providers that they’re going to need to, they need them to figure out the AI strategy, or else you can’t work with them in the future.
There are others that are waiting to see what’s most effective.
They’ve got to get more work done with a limited budget, and so they’re going to need to be creative about allocating work to different providers.

kp.k: Foundation models may disrupt routine in-house work first
kp.d: Su predicts that foundation-model providers will initially target in-house NDA and simple contract reviews because these are easier than bespoke large-firm work. He speculates that improved contract review could subsequently change M&A due diligence and replace elements of firm services. He recommends firms monitor in-house developments, explicitly distinguishing possible future innovation from current capability.
qs: My instinct is to say that it’s going to start in-house before law firms.
Because law firms do more bespoke work, you’ve got in-house teams that are working on NDA reviews, simple contract reviews.
But as they move up the value chain, as they get better at reviewing contracts, these AI companies, you’re going to start to see different elements of what firms do be potentially replaced.

kp.k: Senior partner rates may rise despite AI uncertainty
kp.d: In the closing forecast, Su distinguishes uncertain AI capabilities and legal-department staffing from his stronger expectation that hourly rates will continue rising. He grounds this prediction in clients’ willingness to pay for senior partners’ valuable judgment and guidance, rather than document production alone. Chagui likewise expects the traditional model to change but expressly declines to predict its precise form.
qs: But what I feel most strongly about is that hourly rates will continue their march upwards.
They are providing legitimate valuable guidance and so that’s not going to change.
I think the traditional model is going to change, but I don’t know exactly how, but it’s changing all the time.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI implementation creates demand for experienced flexible lawyers to support adoption, training and human verification.
pts.d: Andy Chagui describes current Latitude engagements supporting relatively small Big Law knowledge management and innovation teams. Experienced lawyers help train internal platforms and check output accuracy. He says staffing these projects with associates is difficult because nonbillable implementation work competes with billable work. Alex Su adds that even granting associates credit does not necessarily resolve this competition. This is an account of human-supported implementation, not autonomous replacement of lawyers.

pts.k: AI-related assignments can support specialist careers outside traditional legal practice.
pts.d: Alex Su argues that remote, engagement-based work allows lawyers to combine narrow assignments into a viable specialization, including work with newer AI tools that a single employer might not support as a full-time role. Andy Chagui reports an instance of an attorney moving from a temporary AI-related knowledge management assignment to a permanent law firm offer.

pts.k: AI-related uncertainty may increase demand for flexible staffing, but associate displacement is not a settled prediction.
pts.d: Alex Su expects greater demand for alternative staffing resources as uncertainty increases. He explicitly declines to predict what AI will do to associate employment. His instinct is that associates will remain, possibly in smaller numbers or in differently organized roles. He identifies generative and agentic AI alongside flexible talent as pressures requiring firms to reconsider staffing and succession.

pts.k: AI and flexible talent offer alternative ways to perform work beneath senior partners while preserving partner accountability.
pts.d: Alex Su sees a price misalignment in work performed beneath senior partners, particularly work billed by first- and second-year associates. He proposes AI, technology and flexible lawyers as complementary resources supporting partners. His description of outsourced leverage refers to experienced external legal talent rather than full-time associates. He maintains that the firm and partner remain responsible for vetting the people doing the work and accountable to clients; he does not claim that AI itself assumes that accountability.

pts.k: Corporate buyer pressure makes AI strategy and changes to work allocation increasingly important.
pts.d: Alex Su reports that some corporate clients require providers to develop an AI strategy as a condition of future work, while others are waiting for effective approaches to emerge. He predicts that competitive pressure and constrained in-house budgets will require the current model to change over the medium to long term. He reports firms treating AI-related knowledge management and innovation as strategically critical. He provides no concrete example establishing that a company has already replaced outside counsel with AI-enabled insourcing.

pts.k: Foundation-model disruption is likely to begin with routine in-house contracts and potentially extend into law firm work.
pts.d: Alex Su predicts that foundation-model providers and AI companies will first address in-house NDA and simple contract reviews because these are easier than bespoke large-firm services. Conditional on improved contract-review capabilities, he envisages substitution for elements of law firm work, potentially including new approaches to M&A due diligence. He frames this as an instinct and a future possibility, not a demonstrated replacement capability.

pts.k: Senior partner hourly rates may keep rising despite AI-driven change.
pts.d: Alex Su's strongest forecast is continued increases in hourly rates, with his reasoning focused on top partners whose judgment and guidance clients value. He distinguishes that value from merely producing a memo. This is not a prediction that all legal work will command higher prices, nor a claim that AI will eliminate hourly billing.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of client conversations, staffing experience and individual placement examples; market forecasts are explicitly judgmental.
pts.d: Chagui and Su speak from their roles at Latitude, a flexible legal talent provider serving firms and corporate legal departments. Implementation claims draw on current engagements and reported demand. Career claims include one permanent-offer example at an AmLaw 100 firm. Pricing and buyer-pressure claims rely on reported client conversations. Su explains that he checks industry reporting against anecdotes from Latitude colleagues. No systematic adoption data, model benchmarks, measured productivity improvements, ROI estimates or quantified AI employment effects are supplied. Future substitution and rate claims are predictions rather than measured findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current implementation experience is distinguished from medium- to long-term market change and highly uncertain staffing outcomes.
pts.d: In this 2026 transcript, the speakers describe AI support assignments, client demands and the career-placement example as current or recent. Flexible staffing is useful where implementation workloads fluctuate and do not justify full-time hiring. Su places broader business-model change in the medium to long term without a calendar deadline. Movement into higher-value firm work depends on AI improving at contract review. The closing rate forecast answers a question about the coming months to years but supplies no precise date or magnitude. Both speakers qualify broader predictions: Chagui cannot specify how the traditional model will change, and Su emphasizes uncertainty about AI capability and legal-department staffing.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The discussion concerns commercial legal providers, experienced and junior lawyers, and corporate legal buyers.
pts.d: Big Law knowledge management and innovation teams gain external implementation capacity and human verification support. Associates face competing billable-work and AI-development demands, alongside uncertain changes to future numbers and organization. Experienced lawyers gain AI-related specialist assignments and potential knowledge management careers. Partners may use different supporting resources while retaining client accountability and, in Su's forecast, pricing power. Corporate legal departments face budget pressure and may adopt routine contract AI before firms, changing provider allocation. Flexible talent providers may see increased demand; foundation-model and legal-AI vendors may extend into additional tasks. The source does not make concrete claims about public access to justice or unmet civil legal need.
